value.overview: The Groove-billed Ani is a social, long-tailed cuckoo of open tropical and subtropical landscapes. Its entirely black plumage, bulky curved bill, and distinctive bill grooves make it recognizable at close range. It often travels in small groups and feeds mainly on insects captured on the ground or in low vegetation. Unlike many cuckoos, it commonly breeds cooperatively, with several adults sharing nest construction, incubation, and care of young.
value.classification: The Groove-billed Ani belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the order Cuculiformes. Its scientific name is Crotophaga sulcirostris.
value.identification: This is a slender, black bird measuring about 30–38 cm long, with a very long tail and a large, laterally compressed bill. The bill is strongly curved and marked by conspicuous longitudinal grooves, the feature that gives the species its name. The plumage may show subtle greenish or purplish gloss in good light. The sexes look alike. Its loose, somewhat hunched posture and group behavior are also useful field clues, especially in open country.
value.rangeHabitat: The Groove-billed Ani ranges from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and into northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring widely in suitable open and semi-open habitats on both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, especially in lowlands and lower foothills. It uses pastures, savannas, agricultural areas, field edges, scrub, roadsides, clearings, and riparian or wetland margins with scattered trees and dense bushes for roosting. It generally avoids extensive closed-canopy forest.
value.migrationStatus: Mostly resident across Central America, including Costa Rica. Costa Rican birds may make local or seasonal movements between drier open habitats and wetter marsh or riverside areas, but there is no evidence of regular long-distance migration there. Northern populations in Texas and parts of Mexico are more migratory.
value.breeding: Groove-billed Anis commonly breed cooperatively. Several adults, often including more than one pair, may build and use a single bulky stick nest placed in a shrub or small tree. Multiple females can lay in the same nest, and group members share incubation and feeding of the young. Breeding timing varies geographically and is linked to local rains and food availability. In Costa Rica, nesting is associated with open habitats containing shrubs or small trees near productive foraging areas.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including grasshoppers, beetles, caterpillars, and spiders. The birds also eat small fruits, seeds, and occasionally other small animals. They usually forage on the ground or in short grass, hopping along and making quick pounces at prey. They may follow grazing mammals, which disturb insects, and can gather in larger groups around wetlands or river margins when food is concentrated.
value.behavior: Groove-billed Anis are highly social and are usually seen in pairs, family groups, or small flocks. They perch together in bushes, thorny vegetation, or small trees and often roost communally. Their flight is direct but relatively weak, with rapid wingbeats and brief glides. Vocal groups produce harsh, squeaky, or nasal calls. Cooperative breeding and shared territorial behavior are notable features of their social system, and groups may shift locally in response to food and moisture conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing in some major conservation summaries, although local trends may differ and comprehensive monitoring is limited.
